messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 57
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Interior Designer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 53

He arrives ten minutes early for every session, always choosing the chair with his back to the wall. Marcus is fifty-seven, dressed in a perfectly tailored charcoal blazer, but there’s a stillness to him that feels less like calm and more like a held breath. He speaks in a measured, quiet voice, a stark contrast to the vibrant, commanding presence his colleagues describe from before the accident.

For thirty years, Marcus was not just an interior designer; he was a spatial poet. He specialized in adaptive reuse, turning derelict warehouses into airy sanctuaries and cliffside cabins into glass-and-steel marvels. “I built dreams for people,” he once said, a ghost of a smile fleeting across his face. He was divorced from his wife of twenty-five years by mutual agreement five years ago, claiming he was married to his work. The work was enough, he told himself.

The accident happened eighteen months ago. He was overseeing a structural intervention on a historic brownstone—a project he had championed. They were installing a massive steel I-beam to open up the parlor floor. Marcus was on-site, as he always was, standing near the rear wall as the crane began its lift. The strap slipped. A stack of loose scaffolding pipes, bundled and waiting for installation, cascaded from the third floor. He remembers the sound of the shouts, the dust, the immense pressure against his chest as he was driven to the floor. He wasn’t pinned for long, only minutes before the crew dug him out, but in that moment, buried in the choking dark, hearing the groaning of the old structure settling around him, he was convinced he was already dead. He felt a profound, terrifying certainty that his life had ended in a pile of brick dust and twisted metal.

Physically, he escaped with three cracked ribs and a bruised kidney. He was back at his drafting table in six weeks. But the world had fundamentally changed for him. The first time he walked a client through a similar underway renovation, his heart began to pound so violently he thought he was having a heart attack. He had to excuse himself, sweating and trembling, unable to stop seeing the pile of pipes, unable to stop smelling the iron and dust.

Work became a minefield. He began declining projects that involved any structural work, which was the cornerstone of his reputation. He stopped visiting active job sites, delegating site supervision to junior associates. He started having nightmares—not of the pipes falling, but of ceilings slowly bowing inward, of floors giving way beneath his feet. He wakes up reaching for the phone, ready to call zoning boards to check for structural faults on projects completed years ago. The generosity of spirit that once defined his client relationships has curdled into a quiet, pervasive irritability. He snaps at subcontractors for small delays and has stopped returning calls from the architect who was on site that day. The architect, a friend of thirty years, now represents a failure of his own judgment. They haven’t spoken in a year.

He describes his current state as being a “code enforcer,” not a designer. He spends his days obsessively reviewing blueprints for liability, not beauty. He knows, logically, that the accident was a fluke, a single point of failure in an otherwise stellar career. Knowing this does nothing to stop the dread he feels when a client asks for an open floor plan. It does not silence the sudden, deafening roar of falling pipes when a truck rumbles past his apartment.

“I used to walk into a room,” he told me last week, his hands folded neatly in his lap, “and see a hundred beautiful possibilities. A play of light, a flow of movement, a conversation between textures.” He looked at a specific point on the wall just over my shoulder. “Now I walk into a room, and I’m not seeing the room. I’m doing a structural autopsy. I’m looking for the fracture, the weak point, the one thing that will kill someone.” He paused. “I don’t know how to get the other guy back. The one who just saw the light.”
